subject: medicine
title: Aortic dissection, thoracic aortic syndromes, and peripheral arterial disease

steps.tx: A breach in the aortic intima allowing blood to enter the media and cleave the vascular wall constitutes a vascular emergency. Developing acute **aortic dissection** is driven primarily by long-standing systemic hypertension and cystic medial necrosis from Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. Patients present with sudden, excruciating tearing or ripping retrosternal chest pain that characteristically radiates to the interscapular region of the back. Pulsatile blood dissects along the media, creating a false lumen that can compress branch arteries or rupture.
steps.say: A tear in the aortic intima allowing blood to penetrate the media constitutes an acute vascular emergency. Developing aortic dissection is driven by chronic hypertension and connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome. Patients experience sudden, excruciating tearing chest pain radiating between the shoulder blades. High-pressure blood dissects through the media, creating a false channel that can compress branches or rupture.

nodes.label: Chronic hypertension and cystic medial necrosis
Intimal tear in ascending or descending aorta
High-pressure false lumen dissects through media

steps.tx: Anatomical localization of the intimal tear dictates emergency surgical versus medical triage. The widely utilized **Stanford classification** categorizes dissections based on involvement of the ascending aorta. Stanford Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta, regardless of the site of the primary intimal tear, and represent surgical emergencies requiring immediate cardiopulmonary bypass repair. Stanford Type B dissections involve only the descending aorta distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery and are initially managed medically.
steps.say: Anatomical location of the intimal tear dictates whether emergency surgery or medical therapy is required. The Stanford classification divides dissections based on involvement of the ascending aorta. Type A dissections involve the ascending aorta and represent surgical emergencies requiring immediate operative repair. Type B dissections originate distal to the left subclavian artery and are initially treated with intensive medical therapy.

rows: Ascending aorta involved (with or without descending)
Mortality 1% to 2% per hour if untreated
Descending aorta only (distal to left subclavian)
Originates in ascending, propagates to descending
Confined exclusively to the ascending aorta
Emergency surgical resection of ascending aorta
High risk of acute aortic regurgitation

steps.tx: Physical examination in acute aortic dissection reveals distinctive vascular and auscultatory signs of proximal or distal extension. Proximal dissection into the aortic root causes acute aortic regurgitation with an early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure. Dissection across major aortic branches produces a marked **pulse deficit** between the arms or blood pressure disparity exceeding twenty millimetres of mercury. Retrograde dissection into the pericardial reflection leads to hemopericardium and acute cardiac tamponade.
steps.say: Bedside examination in aortic dissection demonstrates distinctive vascular and auscultatory signs of extension. Proximal dissection into the valve root causes acute aortic regurgitation with an early diastolic murmur. Occlusion of branch arteries produces a pulse deficit between the limbs or blood pressure disparity over twenty millimetres of mercury. Retrograde rupture into the pericardial space causes cardiac tamponade.

steps.tx: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography of the chest and abdomen is the diagnostic investigation of choice in haemodynamically stable patients. The pathognomonic radiological finding is an **intimal flap** that separates the true lumen from the false lumen. The true lumen typically displays smooth borders and continuous forward pulsatile flow, while the false lumen is frequently larger, demonstrates delayed contrast opacification, and exhibits internal cobweb signs representing residual strands of cleaved media.
steps.say: Computed tomography angiography represents the diagnostic investigation of choice in stable patients. The pathognomonic finding is a visible intimal flap separating the true lumen from the false channel. The true lumen exhibits smooth walls and forward pulsatile flow, whereas the false lumen is larger with delayed opacification and media strands termed cobwebs.

steps.tx: Immediate medical management focuses on halting progression of the dissection flap by reducing aortic wall shear stress. Initiating **intravenous beta blockers** such as esmolol or labetalol is the essential first step, targeting a heart rate below sixty beats per minute. Only after achieving adequate heart rate control are vasodilators like nitroprusside or nicardipine added to lower systolic blood pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg, avoiding reflex sympathetic tachycardia that would accelerate dissection propagation.
steps.say: Immediate medical therapy focuses on halting flap progression by minimizing aortic shear stress. Giving intravenous beta blockers like esmolol is the essential first action, aiming for a heart rate below sixty beats per minute. Only after controlling heart rate are vasodilators added to lower systolic pressure to one hundred to one hundred twenty, avoiding reflex tachycardia.

nodes.label: Achieve target systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg

steps.tx: Uncomplicated Stanford Type B dissections respond well to intensive medical anti-impulse therapy, but complications mandate intervention. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is indicated for **complicated Type B dissection**, defined by persistent refractory pain, uncontrolled hypertension, progressive false lumen expansion, or malperfusion of renal, mesenteric, or iliac vessels. Deploying an endovascular stent-graft seals the primary intimal tear, depressurizes the false lumen, and induces false lumen thrombosis while preserving true lumen branch perfusion.
steps.say: Uncomplicated type B dissections respond to intensive medical therapy, but complications require intervention. Endovascular stent repair is indicated for complicated type B disease, marked by refractory pain, uncontrolled hypertension, false lumen expansion or visceral malperfusion. Deploying a covered stent seals the entry tear and depressurises the false channel.

left.title: Uncomplicated Type B
points: No branch vessel ischemia or malperfusion

right.title: Complicated Type B
points: Persistent or recurrent severe tearing pain
Rapid aortic dilatation or periaortic rupture

steps.tx: Systemic atherosclerosis frequently affects the peripheral arterial vasculature of the lower extremities. Developing symptomatic **peripheral arterial disease** presents classically with intermittent claudication, characterized by reproducible cramping pain in the calf, thigh, or buttock triggered by walking and relieved promptly by rest. Critical limb-threatening ischemia represents the end-stage manifestation, characterized by ischemic rest pain in the distal foot, non-healing ulcerations, or frank gangrene requiring urgent revascularization.
steps.say: Atherosclerosis frequently occludes the peripheral arterial circulation of the lower limbs. Developing peripheral arterial disease presents with intermittent claudication, described as cramping muscle pain during walking that resolves with rest. Critical limb-threatening ischaemia represents end-stage disease, featuring rest pain in the toes, non-healing ulcers or gangrene requiring urgent revascularisation.

nodes.label: Ischemic rest pain (worse supine, relieved hanging)
Critical limb ischemia: Ulcers and gangrene

steps.tx: Bedside vascular assessment relies on measuring the ratio of systolic blood pressure at the ankle to that in the arm. Calculating the **ankle brachial index** provides an objective, non-invasive assessment of lower extremity arterial perfusion. A normal resting index ranges between 1.00 and 1.40. An index of 0.90 or less is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease, with values under 0.40 indicating severe ischemia. Values exceeding 1.40 reflect non-compressible, calcified medial arteries common in diabetes and end-stage renal disease.
steps.say: Bedside vascular evaluation relies on comparing the systolic blood pressure in the ankle against the arm. Calculating the ankle-brachial index provides an objective assessment of arterial perfusion. A normal resting value ranges from one point zero to one point four. A ratio of zero point nine or lower establishes the diagnosis, while values under zero point four indicate severe ischaemia.
